report:
Finding: Model B leans toward a “news/blog/webpage boilerplate” mode relative to Model A.

Reasoning from the evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens cluster tightly around two related themes:
  - News/reporting/headline nouns and proper names: “billionaire,” “politicians,” “activists,” “journalists,” “spokesman/spokeswoman,” “chairman,” “legislators,” “Obama,” “metropolitan.”
  - Blog/site chrome and media/navigation terms: “blogs,” “blogger,” “Blog,” “photo,” “video,” “facebook,” “TV,” “ad/ads,” “Mail,” “May/Mar,” “http,” “On,” plus high-frequency formatting tokens like “\n”, “ ”, “(”, “-”, “/”, “1.” Also section headings like “Sports,” “Traffic,” “Fashion,” “Home.”
- These tokens are exactly the kind found in news site front pages, blog indexes, and article headers/sidebars (categories, dates, nav links, media labels).
- The difference norm is overwhelmingly concentrated in late layers (≈18–25) and at the first few positions (p1–p4, and eventually p0), consistent with a high-level “document/page-type” or “headline/front matter” feature that turns on at the start of a snippet.

No other specific objective (e.g., math, coding, instruction-following) is suggested by the evidence. The clearest interpretable content is a stronger bias in Model B toward news/blog website boilerplate and headline-style text.
